answer.text:
## Student Activism and Protests

Ohio Wesleyan students engaged in various forms of protest and activism regarding the Vietnam War. During the 1969 inauguration of University President Thomas Wenzlau, students and faculty staged protests by wearing white armbands with black centers to show recognition for the National Vietnam Moratorium [Source 2]. Students also participated in organized anti-war efforts, such as forming an OWU peace group that allied with the Student Mobilization Committee to End the War in Vietnam [Source 5]. Activities included participating in fasts to raise money for war victims and the poor, organizing taxpayer rallies, and circulating "We Won't Go" statements in which students declared they would refuse induction into the armed services [Source 3].

## Public Statements and Editorial Positions

Student leaders also voiced their concerns through formal channels and public letters. In December 1967, Larry E. Heinzerling, the editor of The Ohio Wesleyan Transcript, joined student body presidents and campus editors from 100 colleges in signing an open letter to President Johnson that questioned the growing U.S. commitment and whether vital interests necessitated the war [Source 7]. Editorial and opinion pieces in the Transcript reflected a similar sense of urgency, arguing that students could no longer remain morally indifferent to the conflict while domestic needs were being neglected [Source 1, Source 8].

answer.text:
## Anti-War Actions in 1968

During 1968, anti-war actions reported by The Transcript were characterized by direct campus demonstrations, civil disobedience, and protests targeting specific individuals and corporations. Students picketed visiting figures like General Curtis LeMay with signs bearing slogans such as "Burn Draft Cards, Not Babies" and walked out of speeches that advocated for the continuous escalation of the war in Vietnam [1968-01-31-28]. Activists also focused heavily on companies involved in military production, such as Dow Chemical, the manufacturer of napalm, resulting in incidents where recruiters were trapped by students and demonstrations took place across multiple university campuses [1968-01-31-28]. Furthermore, large numbers of students turned over their draft cards in Washington, and writers like Howard Zinn defended civil disobedience and citizens taking to the streets due to the perceived failure of legal channels to address the war [1968-01-31-28, 1968-01-10-3].

## Anti-War Actions in 1970

By 1970, the nature of anti-war activities shifted toward structured political campaigns, grassroots community organizing, and financial protests centered on taxes. The Vietnam Moratorium Committee moved away from single monthly protest days to engage in local community organizing, participation in congressional campaigns, and the circulation of "We Won't Go" statements in which students declared their refusal to accept military induction [1970-04-08-18]. Anti-war efforts also included taxpayer rallies held in dozens of major cities and smaller communities to protest the economic toll of the conflict [1970-04-08-18]. On campus, groups like the PAC organized student strikes through class boycotts on "Tax Day" on April 15 to protest war spending, while organizations like the Businessmen's Educational Movement participated in broader anti-war rallies emphasizing that protest was patriotic [1970-04-08-13, 1970-01-28-20].

answer.text:
## Curfews and Residential Rules

Student life for women at Ohio Wesleyan in the 1960s was heavily shaped by university policies and regulations governed by the Association of Women Students [Source 1, Source 3, Source 4, Source 6]. Early in the decade, freshman women faced strict curfews, such as a 10:30 p.m. dormitory return time, which drew student criticism because campus libraries remained open much later [Source 2]. Debates persisted over age requirements and hours, with AWS members arguing that women should reach the legal age of 21 before receiving senior hours privileges [Source 6], though a 1967 proposal allowed senior women under 21 to apply for senior responsibilities privileges [Source 4]. By the fall of 1968, rules became significantly more liberal: freshman women were permitted to stay out until 1:30 a.m. every weekend, sophomores received unlimited 1:30 a.m. hours, and juniors and seniors with parental consent could stay out until 5:30 a.m. any night [Source 1]. Furthermore, AWS launched a study in 1968 to investigate the possibility of allowing women visitation privileges in off-campus men's apartments [Source 3].

## Housing and Campus Culture

Residential and social life underwent structural shifts later in the decade. In the fall of 1968, OWU introduced coeducational residence patterns and coed dining halls to foster social involvement [Source 5]. East-West Residence Hall accommodated 140 men and 230 women, Thomson Hall housed women, and Monnett Hall closed as new housing became available [Source 5]. All dining units transitioned to coed formats that same year [Source 5]. Beyond housing, women actively participated in campus governance by joining committees like the AWS Handbook Revision Committee [Source 8]. Student attitudes and opinions were also a focal point; a 1960 Ethos Test revealed that 81 per cent of female respondents desired to see more male students attending the university, while both men and women heavily prioritized personality and intelligence in potential partners [Source 7].

answer.text:
Campus housing at Ohio Wesleyan included a variety of residence halls, small living units (SLUs), and fraternity houses, alongside policies that evolved over time [Source 1] [Source 3]. In the late 1960s, regulations limited men to fraternity houses and approved private residences, with mandatory dormitory residence enforced for freshman men [Source 1]. Housing crunches sometimes required the university to place students in the Methodist Theological Seminary and the Delaware Inn [Source 1]. By the 1980s, university committees regularly evaluated housing options, considering adjustments to off-campus housing percentages, single rooms, special interest corridors, and the potential closure of Austin and various small living units [Source 3] ![John Smeaton, dean for student life, talks with students at Tuesday's meeting on housing options for next year.](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1983-01-13/images/0001_Page%201_img1.webp).

Small living units played a prominent role in campus residential life, accommodating specialized programs and interest groups. For instance, International House at 88 Oak Hill Ave. served as a women's residence hall before becoming the International House SLU in 1979, and was later renamed Hartupee House in 1988 [Source 5] ![A large stone house with a sign in front identifying it as "HARTUPEE HOUSE".](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1988-04-06/images/0005_Page%205_img3.webp). Other specialized units included the Women's House at 75 Oak Hill Dr. [Source 6], the Health and Fitness House [Source 7], the Peace and Justice House [Source 8], and the Community Service House, which relocated to Benjamin Spencer House after its previous location at 62 University Ave. was demolished for the Campus Center [Source 4] ![Benjamin Spencer House and Community Service House](https://pub-6b4b0bceb63e48c1af6578ad09beb2e5.r2.dev/1990-01-17/images/0003_Page%203_img1.webp).

Fraternity houses also underwent significant transitions. Beta Theta Pi lost its house at 9 Williams Dr. in spring 1983, during which time the building housed Performing Arts and Honors groups [Source 2] [Source 10]. After fulfilling strict membership and financial requirements, Beta regained the house in February 1987, planning fundraising efforts to convert it back from a dorm structure into a fraternity house [Source 2]. Meanwhile, the displaced Performing Arts and Honors programs were granted new houses at 94 University Ave. and 118 University Ave. [Source 10].
